rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed read-only filesystem embedded in systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem type is a free version of the Veritas filesystem. It is the primary filesystem type for HP-UX operating systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Mac OS filesystems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem intended to replace hfs and allows Mac OS filesystems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem type is a journaling filesystem used on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The overlay kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Linux overlay kernel module, commonly called Overlays, is a union mount filesystem. It lets a user overlay one filesystem on another and produces a single unified view.
rules.impact: The overlay kernel module has known vulnerabilities: CVE-2023-32629, CVE-2023-2640, and CVE-2023-0386. Disabling it reduces the local attack surface by removing support for unneeded filesystem types and lowers the risk of unauthorized setuid file execution, improving overall system security.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem type is a compressed read-only filesystem embedded in systems with limited memory. A squashfs image can be used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, it can be disabled.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf filesystem type is the Universal Disk Format used to implement the ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 specifications. It is an open filesystem format for storing data on a wide range of media and is required to support writing DVDs and newer optical discs.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The firewire-core kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: IEEE 1394 (FireWire) is a serial bus standard for high-speed real-time communication.
rules.impact: Disabling FireWire protects the system from exploitation of flaws in its implementation.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: USB drives provide a means of transferring and storing files, so those files stay persistent and available regardless of network connectivity. Their popularity and usefulness have made USB-based malware a simple and common way to enter a network and a first step toward a persistent threat in the network environment.
rules.impact: Restricting USB access to the system reduces the device's physical attack surface and reduces possible vectors for introducing malware.

rules.title: The unused filesystems kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: Filesystem kernel modules are pieces of code that can be loaded dynamically into the Linux kernel to extend the capabilities of the filesystem, or of the so-called base operating-system kernel. They are typically used to add support for new hardware (as device drivers) or to add system calls.
rules.impact: Loadable filesystem kernel modules are a convenient way to modify a running kernel, but on a compromised system attackers can abuse them to hide processes or files and retain control, and many rootkits use them this way. Removing support for unneeded filesystem types reduces the local attack surface, so disable a type that is not needed; the following filesystem kernel modules have CVEs and should be unavailable unless dependencies exist: ceph — CVE-2022-0670, cifs — CVE-2022-29869, exfat CVE-2022-29973, ext CVE-2022-1184, fat CVE-2022-22043, fscache CVE-2022-3630, fuse CVE-2023-0386, gfs2 CVE-2023-3212, nfs_common CVE-2023-6660, nfsd CVE-2022-43945, smbfs_common CVE-2022-2585.

rules.title: /tmp is tmpfs or a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-accessible directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Making /tmp its own filesystem lets an administrator set additional mount options, such as noexec, which makes /tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a setuid system program and waiting for that program to be updated.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/fstab or systemd unit tmp.mount

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot run executable binaries from /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is tmpfs or a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is a world-accessible directory that can function as shared memory and facilitate inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Making /dev/shm its own filesystem lets an administrator set additional mount options, such as noexec, which makes /dev/shm useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a setuid system program and waiting for that program to be updated.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /dev/shm filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create special devices in /dev/shm partitions.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the filesystem prevents users from introducing privileged programs into the system and prevents non-root users from executing them.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the filesystem prevents users from executing programs from shared memory. This stops users from introducing potentially malicious software into the system.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to support the disk space needs of local users.
rules.impact: The default installation creates only a single / partition. Because /home contains user-created data, there is a risk of resource exhaustion: that data has the entire disk available, which can fill up and affect the system as a whole.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /home partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /home.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /home partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is intended only for storing user files, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /home.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be world-writable.
rules.impact: Placing /var on a separate partition lets an administrator set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system, and other options allow specific behavior to be defined.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var filesystem is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a world-accessible directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications. Temporary files in /var/tmp should persist across reboots.
rules.impact: Making /var/tmp its own filesystem lets an administrator set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot run executable binaries from /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: Making /var/log its own filesystem lets an administrator set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is intended only for log files, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is intended only for log files, set this option so that users cannot run executable binaries from /var/log.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The audit daemon, auditd, stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: Making /var/log/audit its own filesystem lets an administrator set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option specifies that the filesystem cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is intended only for audit logs, set this option so that users cannot run executable binaries from /var/log/audit.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM package manager implements GPG key signing to verify package integrity during and after installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that updates are obtained from a valid source, to protect against tampering that could lead to unintended installation of malware on the system. To do this, make sure GPG keys are configured correctly for the system.

rules.title: The gpgcheck is configured
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck option controls signature verification of packages after download.
rules.impact: It is important to always verify an RPM package signature before installation to ensure the software was obtained from a trusted source.

rules.title: The repo_gpgcheck is configured
rules.explanation: The repo_gpgcheck parameter in the [main] section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and in /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo enables GPG signature verification of repository metadata.
rules.impact: Without repository metadata signature verification, an attacker can substitute packages and their dependencies.

rules.title: The package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems must have repositories configured for the appropriate package managers so the system can receive the latest fixes and updates.
rules.impact: If the system's package repositories are configured incorrectly, important fixes may not be identified, or a fraudulent repository may introduce compromised software.

rules.title: The weak dependencies are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM packaging specification allows three levels of dependencies to be declared: hard dependencies and weak dependencies.
rules.impact: If the system does not require the additional capabilities provided by weak dependencies, it is recommended not to install those packages, in order to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: Security vulnerabilities and functional improvements are regularly addressed through software updates and fixes.
rules.impact: Unpatched software can expose systems to known vulnerabilities that attackers may exploit. It is recommended to apply operating system updates for enterprise assets through automated patch management monthly or more often.

rules.title: SELinux is installed
rules.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control (MAC).
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system installed, only the default discretionary access control system is available.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: Configure SELINUX to be enabled at boot and ensure it has not been overridden by grub boot parameters.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot in the grub configuration so that the controls it provides are not overridden.

rules.title: SELinux policy is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to meet or exceed the default targeted policy, which confines daemons and system software.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary from site to site, and some sites may require a stricter policy than the default, which is acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that at least the recommended default requirements are met.

rules.title: The SELinux mode is not disabled
rules.explanation: SELinux can run in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing.
rules.impact: Running SELinux in disabled mode is strongly discouraged: the system not only avoids enforcing SELinux policy but also avoids labeling persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux later more difficult.

rules.title: The SELinux mode is enforcing
rules.explanation: SELinux can run in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing.
rules.impact: Running SELinux in disabled mode means the system neither enforces SELinux policy nor labels persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux later more difficult. Permissive mode is useful for developing SELinux policy, but it only logs access-denial records and does not prevent any operations.

rules.title: No unconfined services exist
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined domains.
rules.impact: SELinux policy rules apply to unconfined processes, but policy rules allow processes running in unconfined domains almost any access, so those processes rely largely on DAC rules; if an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux will not prevent an attacker from gaining access to system resources and data, although DAC rules still apply. SELinux is an additional security control on top of DAC rules and does not replace them.

rules.title: The MCS Translation Service (mcstrans) is not installed
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon provides category label information to client processes that request it. Label translations are defined in /etc/selinux/targeted/setrans.conf.
rules.impact: Because this service is not used very often, remove it to reduce the amount of potentially vulnerable code running on the system.

rules.title: SETroubleshoot is not installed
rules.explanation: The SETroubleshoot service notifies desktop users of SELinux denials through a convenient interface. The service provides important information about configuration errors, unauthorized intrusions, and other potential errors.
rules.impact: The SETroubleshoot service is an unnecessary daemon to run on a server, especially if X Windows is disabled.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password requires anyone who reboots the system to enter a password before they can set boot command-line parameters.
rules.impact: Requiring a boot password when the bootloader starts prevents an unauthorized user from entering boot parameters or changing the boot partition. This prevents users from weakening security, for example by disabling SELinux at boot.

rules.title: The access to bootloader config is configured
rules.explanation: The grub files contain information about boot settings and passwords for unlocking boot options.
rules.impact: Setting read and write permissions for root only prevents non-root users from viewing boot parameters or changing them. Non-root users who read boot parameters may identify boot-time security weaknesses and exploit them.

rules.title: The authentication is required when booting into rescue mode
rules.explanation: Rescue mode boots the system with a minimal set of services and provides an administrator console.
rules.impact: Without a password prompt, anyone with access to the console gets a root shell, bypassing the normal login procedure.

rules.title: The authentication is required when booting into emergency mode
rules.explanation: Emergency mode boots the system with a minimal set of services and provides an administrator console.
rules.impact: Without a password prompt, anyone with access to the console gets a root shell, bypassing the normal login procedure.

rules.title: The systemd ability to spawn an interactive boot process is disabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter systemd.confirm_spawn makes systemd request interactive confirmation before starting each service at boot.
rules.impact: Interactive boot allows a person with console access to influence which services are started and to interfere with the boot process.

rules.title: The fs.protected_hardlinks is configured
rules.explanation: fs.protected_hardlinks controls the creation of hard links to files.
rules.impact: Disallowing hard links eliminates vulnerabilities based on unsafe filesystems accessed by privileged programs. This reduces the risk of an exploitation vector that uses an unsafe open or creat.

rules.title: The fs.protected_symlinks is configured
rules.explanation: fs.protected_symlinks controls how the kernel handles symbolic links.
rules.impact: Disallowing symbolic links eliminates vulnerabilities based on unsafe filesystems accessed by privileged programs. This reduces the risk of an exploitation vector that uses an unsafe open or creat.

rules.title: The fs.suid_dumpable is configured
rules.explanation: fs.suid_dumpable determines whether a privileged process can generate a core dump.
rules.impact: Core dumps can contain sensitive data in memory, such as password hashes or keys. An attacker could potentially use this to gain access to that data.

rules.title: The kernel.dmesg_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: kernel.dmesg_restrict can be used to configure the Linux kernel and prevent unprivileged users from accessing information from the kernel log buffer.
rules.impact: Restricting access to the kernel message buffer limits access to root only. This prevents attackers from obtaining additional system information as unprivileged users.

rules.title: The kernel.kptr_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: kernel.kptr_restrict sets whether disclosure of kernel addresses through /proc and other interfaces should be restricted.
rules.impact: Masking kernel symbols in /proc/kallsys reduces an attacker's ability to use them to gain more information about what to attack on the system.

rules.title: The kernel.randomize_va_space is configured
rules.explanation: ASLR is a technique that reduces the impact of vulnerability exploitation by randomly arranging the address space of a process's key data areas.
rules.impact: Random placement of virtual memory areas makes it harder to write exploits for memory pages, because memory placement continually shifts.

rules.title: The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace() system call provides a means by which one process can observe and control the execution of another process, and examine and modify the memory and registers of the traced process.
rules.impact: If one application is compromised, an attacker can attach to other running processes to extract additional credentials and continue expanding the attack. Enabling restricted mode limits a compromised process's ability to attach to other processes running as the same user.

rules.title: The core file size is configured
rules.explanation: core limits the core file size; hard enforces hard resource limits.
rules.impact: Setting a hard limit on core dumps prevents the user from overriding the soft variable. A core dump includes a memory image taken when the operating system terminates an application; the image may contain sensitive data and is usually useful only to developers debugging problems.

rules.title: The systemd-coredump ProcessSizeMax is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is usually used to determine why a program crashed, and it can also be used to extract confidential information from the core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is usually useful only to developers debugging problems, which increases risk to the system.

rules.title: The systemd-coredump Storage is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is usually used to determine why a program crashed, and it can also be used to extract confidential information from the core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image taken when the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is usually useful only to developers debugging problems.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy is not legacy
rules.explanation: The system-wide LEGACY cryptographic policy allows obsolete protocols and algorithms (TLS 1.0/1.1, SSH2, DSA, 3DES, RC4).
rules.impact: The LEGACY policy allows the use of cryptographically weak algorithms and protocols.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy disables sha1 hash and signature support
rules.explanation: SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm) is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit hash value.
rules.impact: The SHA-1 hash function has a weak construction, and advances in cryptanalysis have made it vulnerable to attack; the most serious danger is a collision, which occurs when two different pieces of data produce the same hash value, and this hash algorithm has been considered weak since 2005. Use of SHA-1 with hash-based message authentication codes (HMAC) does not depend on the collision resistance of the corresponding hash function, so recent attacks on SHA-1 have significantly less impact on the use of SHA-1 for HMAC, and for that reason the hmac-sha1 MAC is not disabled.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy macs are configured
rules.explanation: A MAC algorithm can be used to provide data-origin authentication and data integrity protection.
rules.impact: Weak algorithms continue to draw attention as a weakness that can be exploited with greater computing power. An attacker who has broken the algorithm can use a MITM position to decrypt the tunnel and capture credentials and information.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy disables cbc for ssh
rules.explanation: CBC mode is an algorithm that uses a block cipher.
rules.impact: A vulnerability in SSH messages that use CBC mode can allow an attacker to recover plaintext from a ciphertext block.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy disables chacha20-poly1305 for ssh
rules.explanation: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) algorithm that combines the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 message authentication code. Its use in IETF protocols is standardized in RFC 8439.
rules.impact: ChaCha20-Poly1305 has a vulnerability identified as CVE-2023-48795.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy disables EtM for ssh
rules.explanation: Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) mode in SSH is vulnerable to the attack described in CVE-2023-48795 (Terrapin).
rules.impact: Using EtM in SSH allows an attacker to carry out a Terrapin attack and weaken protection of the channel.

rules.title: The system wide crypto policy enables post-quantum algorithms
rules.explanation: The PQ subpolicy adds post-quantum algorithms to the system-wide cryptographic policy.
rules.impact: Without post-quantum algorithms, traffic protected by current key exchanges can be decrypted in the future by an adversary with a quantum computer.

rules.title: /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and function as a message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users attempting to log in of their legal status regarding the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any monitoring policies in effect. Displaying operating-system and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to use specific exploits against the system.

rules.title: /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before login on local terminals.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users attempting to log in of their legal status regarding the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any monitoring policies in effect. Displaying operating-system and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to use specific exploits against the system.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users attempting to log in of their legal status regarding the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any monitoring policies in effect. Displaying operating-system and patch-level information in login banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to use specific exploits against the system.

rules.title: The access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and function as a message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have access configured correctly, unauthorized users can modify it with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before login on local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have access configured correctly, unauthorized users can modify it with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue.net does not have access configured correctly, unauthorized users can modify it with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME display manager that handles graphical login for GNOME-based systems. Lock mode in dconf can be used to prevent users from changing certain settings.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users attempting to log in of their legal status regarding the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any monitoring policies in effect. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: GDM disable-user-list is configured
rules.explanation: GDM handles graphical login for GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list parameter controls whether the user list is displayed on the login screen.
rules.impact: Displaying the user list removes half of the user ID/password equation an unauthorized person would need in order to log in. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: GDM screen lock is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Desktop Manager can automatically lock the screen when a user is idle for a specified period of time.
rules.impact: Setting a lock value reduces the window of opportunity for a user to gain unauthorized access to another user's session that was left unattended. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: GDM automount is configured
rules.explanation: By default, GNOME automatically mounts removable media when it is inserted, for user convenience.
rules.impact: With automatic mounting enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and its contents become available on the system, even if they did not have permission to mount it. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never is configured
rules.explanation: The autorun-never parameter allows GNOME Display Manager to disable autorun through GDM.
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can use autorun features when the media is inserted into the system and then execute. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: The X Display Manager Control Protocol (XDMCP) is intended to provide authenticated access to display management services for remote displays.
rules.impact: XDMCP is inherently insecure: it is not an encrypted protocol, so an attacker may intercept keystrokes entered by the user, and it is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks that can allow an attacker to steal legitimate users' credentials by impersonating the XDMCP server.

rules.title: Wayland is configured
rules.explanation: GDM can be configured to disable Wayland through the WaylandEnable=false parameter in custom.conf.
rules.impact: Disabling Wayland moves the session to X11, which does not isolate clients from each other or from the X server.

rules.title: The autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs allows devices to be mounted automatically, typically including CD/DVD and USB drives.
rules.impact: With automatic mounting enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and its contents become available on the system, even if they did not have permission to mount it.

rules.title: The avahi daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a system for service discovery over multicast DNS/DNS-SD. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on the local network without any specific configuration.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is usually not required for system functionality. It is recommended to remove this package to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: avahi package and avahi-daemon.socket, avahi-daemon.service status

rules.title: The cockpit web services are not in use
rules.explanation: The cockpit web services provide the ability to administer the system remotely through a web browser.
rules.impact: If there is no local-site-approved requirement for remote web administration of the system, the cockpit web server packages should be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: cockpit-ws package and cockpit.socket, cockpit.service status

rules.title: The dhcp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: DHCP is a service that allows machines to be assigned IP addresses dynamically.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically configured as a DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the kea package to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: kea package and kea-dhcp*, kea-dhcp-ddns.service status

rules.title: The dns server services are not in use
rules.explanation: DNS is a hierarchical naming system that maps names to IP addresses for computers, services, and other resources connected to a network.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically intended to operate as a DNS server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight tool that provides DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and DHCP services.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically intended to operate as a DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and/or DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows workstations.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and filesystems on Windows systems, this package can be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The ftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (it allows anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: dovecot and cyrus-imapd are open-source IMAP and POP3 server packages for Linux-based systems.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers will not be provided by this system, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: dovecot and cyrus-imapd packages and their service status

rules.title: The network file system services are not in use
rules.explanation: NFS is one of the earliest and most widely deployed filesystems in the UNIX environment. It provides the ability for systems to mount filesystems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not require access to network shares, or the ability to provide network filesystem services for network resources of other hosts, it is recommended to remove the nfs-utils package to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: The print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS provides the ability to print to both local and network printers. A system running CUPS can also accept print jobs from remote systems and print them on local printers, and it also provides remote administration through a web interface.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to print jobs or accept print jobs from other systems, it is recommended to remove CUPS to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: cups package and cups.socket, cups.service status

rules.title: The rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on, and the rpcbind service redirects the client to the correct port number so it can communicate with the requested service. Portmapper is an RPC service used to map other RPC services to the corresponding port numbers on the server.
rules.impact: A small request sent to Portmapper generates a large response, which makes it a suitable tool for DDoS attacks. If rpcbind is not required, it is recommended to remove the rpcbind package to reduce the potential attack surface.
rules.scope: rpcbind package and rpcbind.socket, rpcbind.service status

rules.title: The rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service can be used to synchronize files between systems over network links.
rules.impact: If this is not required, the rsync-daemon package should be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. The rsyncd service presents a security threat because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.
rules.scope: rsync-daemon package and rsyncd.socket, rsyncd.service status

rules.title: The snmp services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is a widely used protocol for monitoring the status of network equipment, computer equipment, and devices such as uninterruptible power supplies.
rules.impact: An SNMP server can use SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and does not require authentication to execute commands. If the SNMP service is not required, the net-snmp package should be removed to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: The telnet server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems through the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Someone who can analyze network traffic can steal credentials, while the ssh package provides an encrypted session and stronger security.

rules.title: The tftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP machines. A TFTP server lets a TFTP client connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to run as a TFTP server, remove the package to reduce the attack surface. TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication.
rules.scope: tftp-server package and tftp.socket, tftp.service status

rules.title: The web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions and environments.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically configured as a proxy server, remove the squid package to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers provide a way to host website content.
rules.impact: If the local site has no approved requirement to run a web server service, remove web server packages to reduce the attack surface.
rules.scope: httpd and nginx packages and their service status

rules.title: The mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs) such as sendmail and Postfix listen for incoming mail and deliver messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If the system is not meant to be a mail server, configure the MTA to handle only local mail.
rules.impact: Mail transfer agent software is complex, and most implementations have a long history of security problems. The system should still handle local mail, but the MTA daemon does not need to listen on a port unless the server is meant to receive and process mail from other systems.

rules.title: A graphical user interface is not in use
rules.explanation: Server systems should not include a graphical environment: it increases the attack surface and is not needed for server tasks.
rules.impact: An installed graphical interface adds services and applications that may contain vulnerabilities and are not required on a server.

rules.title: X window server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface in which users can run programs in multiple windows and use various extensions.
rules.impact: If the organization does not specifically require graphical login through X Window, remove it to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: Xwayland is not in use
rules.explanation: The xorg-x11-server-Xwayland package provides X11 compatibility inside a Wayland session.
rules.impact: Xwayland expands the attack surface of the graphical subsystem when graphics are not required on the server.

rules.title: Only approved services are listening on a network interface
rules.explanation: A network port is identified by its number, the associated IP address, and the communication protocol, such as TCP or UDP. A listening port is an endpoint where an application or process accepts incoming packets from remote locations, and a firewall can leave that port open or closed (filtered).
rules.impact: Services listening on the system are a potential attack vector and should be reviewed. If a service is not required, stop it and remove its package, or stop and mask it when required packages depend on it, to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The ftp client is not installed
rules.explanation: FTP is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (it allows anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or authentication credentials, so use SFTP when file transfer is required. If the system does not need to run as an FTP server, remove the package to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The ldap client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a way to look up information in a central database.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, remove the software to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which lets users connect to other systems over the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted, so an unauthorized user can steal credentials from an unencrypted transmission. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and stronger security.

rules.title: The tftp client is not installed
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP machines. A TFTP server lets a TFTP client connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication.

rules.title: The time synchronization is in use
rules.explanation: System time should be synchronized across all systems in the environment. This is usually done by establishing an authoritative time server, or a set of servers, and synchronizing every system clock to them.
rules.impact: Time synchronization supports time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos and keeps log timestamps consistent across the enterprise, which helps forensic investigations.

rules.title: The chrony is configured
rules.explanation: The server directive names an NTP server that can be used as a time source. The pool directive names a pool of NTP servers rather than a single NTP server.
rules.impact: Time synchronization supports time-sensitive security mechanisms and keeps timestamps in log files consistent across the enterprise for forensic investigations.

rules.title: The chrony is not run as the root user
rules.explanation: The file /etc/sysconfig/chronyd sets options for chrony, including the user chrony runs as. By default that user is chrony.
rules.impact: Services should not run as the root user.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon runs batch jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Even when the system has no user jobs that must run, it has maintenance tasks that may include security monitoring, and cron is used to run them.

rules.title: The access to /etc/crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/crontab is used by cron to manage its own jobs.
rules.impact: This file lists the system jobs that cron runs. Write access can let unprivileged users raise their privileges, and read access can reveal those jobs and a way to gain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.hourly is configured
rules.explanation: This directory contains system cron jobs that are meant to run hourly.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.daily is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that are meant to run daily.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.weekly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that are meant to run weekly.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.monthly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains system cron jobs that are meant to run monthly.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.yearly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.yearly directory contains system cron jobs that are meant to run yearly.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.d is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that run like the hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but need finer control of when they run.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory for unprivileged users can give them a way to gain unauthorized elevated privileges. Read access can show an unprivileged user how to gain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to crontab is configured
rules.explanation: crontab is the program used to install, remove, or list the tables that control the cron daemon.
rules.impact: On many systems only the system administrator is allowed to schedule cron jobs. Using the cron.allow file to control who may run cron jobs enforces that policy.

rules.title: The access to at is configured
rules.explanation: at allows fairly complex time specifications, extending the POSIX.2 standard.
rules.impact: On many systems only the system administrator is allowed to schedule at jobs. Using the at.allow file to control who may run at jobs enforces that policy.

rules.title: IPv6 status is identified
rules.explanation: IPv6 is based on 128-bit addressing and can support 340 undecillion unique addresses.
rules.impact: Enable and configure IPv6 unless that conflicts with local site policy.
rules.scope: ipv6 module state and disable_ipv6 sysctl settings

rules.title: The wireless interfaces are not available
rules.explanation: Wireless networking is used when wired networks are unavailable.
rules.impact: If wireless communication is not to be used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology used to exchange data between devices over short distances.
rules.impact: An attacker may find a way to access or damage data. Viruses or other malicious code can also use Bluetooth to infect other devices.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: DCCP is a transport-layer protocol that supports streaming media and telephony.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC is intended to provide communication between cluster nodes.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: RDS is a transport-layer protocol intended to provide low-latency, high-bandwidth communication between cluster nodes.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SCTP is a transport-layer protocol used to support messaging, with multiple message streams in a single connection.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The atm kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: ATM is a protocol that operates at the network, data-link, and physical layers and is based on virtual circuits and virtual paths.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The can kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: CAN is a serial communication protocol originally developed for the automotive industry.
rules.impact: Removing support for unneeded protocols reduces the local attack surface of the system. If this protocol is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.ip_forward is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv4 packets.
rules.impact: Routing protocol daemons are normally used on routers to exchange network topology with other routers, and using that software when it is not required can send system network information across the network unnecessarily. Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces cannot forward IPv4 packets.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts, and a host that is not itself a router does not need to send them. net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Routing protocol daemons are normally used on routers to exchange network topology with other routers. If this capability is used when it is not required, system network information can be sent across the network unnecessarily.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Routing protocol daemons are normally used on routers to exchange network topology with other routers. If this capability is used when it is not required, system network information can be sent across the network unnecessarily.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects controls sending of all IPv4 ICMP redirect packets on all interfaces.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send incorrect ICMP redirects to other routers in an attempt to corrupt routing and make users reach a system set up by the attacker instead of the legitimate system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects controls sending of all IPv4 ICMP redirect packets on a newly added network interface.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send incorrect ICMP redirects to other routers in an attempt to corrupt routing and make users reach a system set up by the attacker instead of the legitimate system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls whether the kernel logs bogus responses that do not comply with RFC-1122 and come from broadcast reframes.
rules.impact: Some routers, and some attackers, send responses that violate RFC-1122 and try to fill the log filesystem with many useless error messages.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls whether all ICMP echo and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses are ignored.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo and timestamp requests sent to broadcast or multicast addresses can make the host start or join a Smurf attack, in which an attacker sends many ICMP broadcasts with a spoofed source so replies return to that address, which is probably not routable. If many hosts reply, the volume of traffic on the network can increase sharply.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell the host, acting as a router, to send packets by an alternate path. net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects controls acceptance of all IPv4 ICMP redirect packets on all interfaces.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell the host, acting as a router, to send packets by an alternate path. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 makes the system reject IPv4 ICMP redirect packets, so outsiders cannot update its routing tables.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and let an external routing device update the system routing tables. net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects controls acceptance of all IPv4 ICMP redirect packets on a newly added network interface, and this recommendation does not apply if the system is a router.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and let an external routing device update the system routing tables. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 makes the system reject IPv4 ICMP redirect messages on a newly added network interface.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are the same as ICMP redirects, except that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 makes the system reject any IPv4 routing-table updates from known gateways that may have been compromised.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. Those gateways are assumed to be known to the system and most likely safe.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 makes the system reject IPv4 routing-table updates from possibly compromised known gateways on a newly added network interface.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter controls reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter to 1 is a good way to stop spoofed packets that cannot be answered from being sent to the system. One case where this feature fails is when asymmetric routing is in use.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter controls reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 is a good way to stop spoofed packets that cannot be answered from being sent to the system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The Accept_source_route option makes network interfaces accept packets with the Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) option set, and net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route controls acceptance of all such IPv4 packets on all interfaces. Source routing lets the sender partly or fully specify the path, unlike packets routed by the network routers, and it is sometimes needed when systems are unreachable from some locations, such as private addresses or Internet-routable addresses.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route to 0 stops the system from accepting source-routed packets. On a system that routes Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another, where those spaces do not route to each other, source-routed packets could otherwise let an attacker using Internet-routable addresses reach private-address systems by specifying a path that routing protocols would not allow.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The Accept_source_route option makes network interfaces accept packets with the Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) option set, and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route controls acceptance of all such IPv4 packets on newly added network interfaces. Source routing lets the sender partly or fully specify the path, unlike packets routed by the network routers, and it is sometimes needed when systems are unreachable from some locations, such as private addresses or Internet-routable addresses.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 stops the system from accepting source-routed packets. On a system that routes Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another, where those spaces do not route to each other, source-routed packets could otherwise let an attacker using Internet-routable addresses reach private-address systems by specifying a path that routing protocols would not allow.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: When enabled, this feature logs packets with unroutable source addresses to the kernel log. net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with unroutable source addresses on any network interface are logged to the kernel log.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians to 1 enables this feature. Logging these packets lets an administrator investigate whether an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: When enabled, this feature logs packets with unroutable source addresses to the kernel log. net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with unroutable source addresses on a newly added network interface are logged to the kernel log.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians to 1 enables this feature. Logging these packets lets an administrator investigate whether an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is configured
rules.explanation: When tcp_syncookies is set, the kernel handles TCP SYN packets normally until the queue of open connections fills, after which SYN cookie behavior takes effect.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN-flood attacks to deny service by sending many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. Setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 1 enables SYN cookies so the system can keep accepting valid connections while under a denial-of-service attack.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet parameter allows routing of loopback addresses in 127.0.0.0/8.
rules.impact: Routing loopback addresses can bypass access restrictions on local services and is used in attacks that redirect traffic.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.route_localnet is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.route_localnet parameter allows routing of loopback addresses in 127.0.0.0/8 for new interfaces.
rules.impact: Routing loopback addresses can bypass access restrictions on local services and is used in attacks that redirect traffic.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv6 packets.
rules.impact: Routing protocol daemons are normally used on routers to exchange network topology with other routers, and using that software when it is not required can send system network information across the network unnecessarily. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces cannot forward IPv6 packets.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding flag tells the system whether it can forward IPv6 on the default network interface or on a newly added one.
rules.impact: Routing protocol daemons are normally used on routers to exchange network topology with other routers. If this software is used when it is not required, system network information can be sent across the network unnecessarily.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects controls acceptance of all IPv6 ICMP redirect packets on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 makes the system reject IPv6 ICMP redirect packets, so outsiders cannot update its routing tables.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and let an external routing device update the system routing tables. net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects controls acceptance of all IPv6 ICMP redirect packets on a newly added network interface, and this recommendation does not apply if IPv6 is disabled or the system is a router.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and let an external routing device update the system routing tables. Setting net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects to 0 makes the system reject IPv6 ICMP redirect messages on a newly added network interface.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The Accept_source_route option makes network interfaces accept packets with the Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) option set, and net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route controls acceptance of all such IPv6 packets on all interfaces. Source routing lets the sender partly or fully specify the path, which is sometimes needed to reach otherwise unreachable systems such as private addresses or Internet-routable addresses, and this recommendation does not apply if IPv6 is disabled.
