On a system that routes Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another, where those spaces do not route to each other, source-routed packets could otherwise let an attacker using Internet-routable addresses reach private-address systems by specifying a path that routing protocols would not allow.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The Accept_source_route option makes network interfaces accept packets with the Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) option set, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route controls acceptance of all such IPv6 packets on newly added network interfaces. Source routing lets the sender partly or fully specify the path, which is sometimes needed to reach otherwise unreachable systems such as private addresses or Internet-routable addresses, and this recommendation does not apply if IPv6 is disabled.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 stops the system from accepting source-routed packets. On a system that routes Internet-routable addresses on one interface and private addresses on another, where those spaces do not route to each other, source-routed packets could otherwise let an attacker using Internet-routable addresses reach private-address systems by specifying a path that routing protocols would not allow.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement messages to announce that they are available and to give neighboring nodes the information they need to configure themselves on the network. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra controls acceptance of any IPv6 RA messages on any network device.
rules.impact: Systems should not accept router advertisements, because they can be tricked into routing traffic to compromised machines.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce that they are available and to give neighboring nodes the information they need to configure themselves on the network. net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra controls acceptance of IPv6 RA messages on newly added network devices.
rules.impact: Systems should not accept router advertisements, because they can be tricked into routing traffic to compromised machines.

rules.title: The firewalld is installed
rules.explanation: firewalld is a high-level utility for managing firewall rules. It does not filter packets itself and relies on the nftables subsystem in the Linux kernel.
rules.impact: firewalld is a dynamic, user-friendly firewall manager that can protect against threats from the enterprise network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host.

rules.title: The firewalld backend is configured
rules.explanation: The FirewallBackend option selects the backend firewall implementation.
rules.impact: Checking that the backend mechanism is configured correctly preserves critical firewall functionality.

rules.title: The firewalld.service is configured
rules.explanation: firewalld.service is the firewall service daemon that provides a dynamically configurable firewall with a D-Bus interface.
rules.impact: firewalld.service must be active for rules configured through FirewallD to be applied. firewalld.service must be enabled so that it starts automatically after a system reboot.

rules.title: The firewalld active zone target is configured
rules.explanation: FirewallD zones are network or inter-network zones that define the trust level of the interface used for a connection. A zone target can be set to ACCEPT, %%REJECT%%, or DROP.
rules.impact: With a default accept policy, the firewall accepts any packet that is not configured to be rejected. It is easier to allow acceptable use than to block unacceptable use.

rules.title: The firewalld loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: Every device with network capability has a loopback interface. Loopback traffic is network communication in which a device sends data to itself.
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the machine and is usually critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen, and every other interface should ignore traffic on that network as a countermeasure against spoofing.
rules.scope: firewalld zones and rules for the lo interface

rules.title: The firewalld loopback source address traffic is configured
rules.explanation: Every device with network capability has a loopback interface, and loopback traffic is communication in which a device sends data to itself by directing that traffic back to its own network interface. Outbound traffic is data sent from the device to another device or network.
rules.impact: The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen. All other interfaces should ignore traffic on that network as a defense against spoofing.

rules.title: The firewalld services and ports are configured
rules.explanation: Services and ports can be accepted, explicitly rejected, or dropped by a zone.
rules.impact: To reduce the attack surface of the system, all services and ports should be blocked unless they are required.

rules.title: The firewalld default zone is set to drop
rules.explanation: The default firewalld zone defines how inbound traffic is handled on interfaces that are not assigned to other zones.
rules.impact: The drop zone discards all unsolicited inbound traffic, reducing the attack surface of the host.

rules.title: The conflicting firewall utilities are not in use with firewalld
rules.explanation: Running firewalld at the same time as another firewall manager (nftables.service, iptables-services, ufw) causes rule conflicts.
rules.impact: Conflicting managers can overwrite one another's rules and leave the system without the expected traffic filtering.

rules.title: The firewalld logs denied packets
rules.explanation: firewalld can log dropped packets, which makes unwanted and malicious traffic detectable.
rules.impact: Without logging of dropped packets, unauthorized access attempts go unnoticed.

rules.title: The firewalld blocks ICMP timestamp requests and replies
rules.explanation: ICMP timestamp request/reply messages let a remote party determine the system uptime and are used in reconnaissance.
rules.impact: Replies to ICMP timestamp requests reveal information about the system and can be used to bypass time-based filtering.

rules.title: The access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/ssh/sshd_config and files ending in .conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory contain configuration specifications for sshd.
rules.impact: Configuration specifications for sshd must be protected from unauthorized changes by unprivileged users.

rules.title: The access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ directory is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ directory contains drop-in configuration files for the SSH server.
rules.impact: Weak permissions allow the SSH server configuration to be changed and remote-access protections to be weakened.

rules.title: The access to SSH private host key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH private key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In that method, possession of the private key is proof of identity.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the host SSH private key file, the host can be compromised.

rules.title: The access to SSH public host key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user modifies the host public key file, the SSH service can be compromised.

rules.title: The sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: This variable limits the ciphers that SSH can use during communication.
rules.impact: Weak ciphers used for authentication to a cryptographic module cannot provide confidentiality or integrity, and system data can be compromised.

rules.title: The sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: Key exchange is any cryptographic method by which cryptographic keys are exchanged between two parties, allowing a cryptographic algorithm to be used.
rules.impact: Key-exchange methods that are considered weak should be removed. A method may be considered weak if it uses too few bits or if the hash algorithm is considered too weak, and weak algorithms can leave connections exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: The sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: This variable limits the types of MAC algorithms that SSH can use during communication.
rules.impact: MD5 and 96-bit MAC algorithms are considered weak and have been shown to increase exploitability in SSH downgrade attacks. Weak algorithms continue to draw attention as a weak point that can be exploited with greater computing power.

rules.title: The sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: Parameters are available to restrict the users and groups that can access the system through SSH.
rules.impact: Restricting which users can remotely access the system through SSH helps ensure that only authorized users gain access.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config: AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, DenyGroups

rules.title: The sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies the file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is allowed.
rules.impact: Banners warn connecting users about the site policy for the connection. Displaying a warning message before the normal user login can assist prosecution of people who violate the computer system.

rules.title: The sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control the timeout of SSH sessions.
rules.impact: Set appropriate values for both ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax to prevent resource exhaustion. If connections are allowed to stay open indefinitely, that can be used as a DDOS attack, or simple resource exhaustion can occur on unreliable networks.

rules.title: The sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding parameter disables all forwarding features, including X11, ssh-agent, TCP, and StreamLocal.
rules.impact: Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational need to use X11 applications directly. Leaving port forwarding enabled can expose the organization to security risks and to the creation of backdoors.

rules.title: The sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter specifies whether GSSAPI-based user authentication is allowed.
rules.impact: Allowing GSSAPI authentication over SSH exposes the system GSSAPI to remote hosts, and it should be disabled to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication through trusted hosts using .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv is allowed.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: The sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter forces users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH.

rules.title: The sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server.
rules.impact: Setting LoginGraceTime to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.

rules.title: The sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: SSH provides several logging levels with varying degrees of detail.
rules.impact: The INFO level is the basic level and records only SSH user login activity. The VERBOSE level records login and logout activity and the key fingerprint of any SSH key used to log in.

rules.title: The sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts allowed per connection.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server.

rules.title: The sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxStartups parameter specifies the maximum number of concurrent unauthenticated connections to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service caused by a large number of pending authentication attempts, use the MaxStartups rate limit to protect the availability of sshd logins and keep the daemon from being overwhelmed.

rules.title: The sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxSessions parameter specifies the maximum number of open sessions allowed for a given connection.
rules.impact: To protect the system from denial of service caused by a large number of concurrent sessions, use the MaxSessions rate limit to protect the availability of sshd logins and keep the daemon from being overwhelmed.

rules.title: The sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server allows login to accounts with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Disallowing remote shell access for accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: The sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user can log in through SSH.
rules.impact: Disabling root logins over SSH requires system administrators to authenticate with their own individual accounts and then elevate privileges to root. This limits the ability to repudiate actions and provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.

rules.title: The sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment option allows users to provide environment settings to the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables through the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security controls.

rules.title: The sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) interface.
rules.impact: When usePAM is set to yes, PAM correctly handles account and session types.

rules.title: The sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows an authorized user to run a command as the superuser or another user, according to the security policy.
rules.impact: The security policy defines which privileges, if any, a user has for running sudo.

rules.title: The access on sudoers configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo configuration files (/etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/*) define who is allowed to run which commands with elevated privileges.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on sudoers allow unrestricted root privileges to be obtained.

rules.title: The access on the /etc/sudoers.d directory is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/sudoers.d/ directory contains additional sudo configuration files.
rules.impact: Write access to the sudoers.d directory allows a custom rule to be added and root privileges to be obtained.

rules.title: The sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal.
rules.impact: Attackers can use sudo to start a malicious program that creates a background process which remains after the main program exits.

rules.title: The sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: The Defaults logfile entry sets the path to the sudo log file.
rules.impact: Defining a dedicated log file for sudo makes it easier to audit sudo commands and to create auditd rules for sudo.

rules.title: The users must provide password for escalation
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users must enter a password for privilege elevation.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users can access resources or perform tasks they are not authorized for. When operating systems provide a way to extend functionality, it is critical that the user re-authenticate.

rules.title: The re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users can re-authenticate for privilege elevation.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users can access resources or perform tasks for which they have no authorization. When operating systems provide a way to extend functionality, it is essential that the user re-authenticate.

rules.title: The sudo pwfeedback is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo pwfeedback option displays asterisks as a password is entered and can lead to a buffer overflow vulnerability.
rules.impact: pwfeedback has historically led to vulnerabilities in the sudo implementation and is not a safe default.

rules.title: The sudo visiblepw is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo visiblepw option allows a password to be entered in clear text when terminal echo cannot be disabled.
rules.impact: Displaying the password on screen exposes credentials to people nearby and in session logs.

rules.title: The sudo timestamp_timeout is configured
rules.explanation: sudo caches used credentials for 5 minutes by default.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged access to another user.

rules.title: The sudo timestamp_type is configured
rules.explanation: The timestamp_type parameter defines the scope of the sudo authentication timestamp (global or limited to the terminal).
rules.impact: A global timestamp allows a previously completed authentication from another session of the same user to be reused.

rules.title: The access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or a shell as another user. Ordinarily, any user can run the su command.
rules.impact: Restricting the use of su and using sudo instead gives system administrators better control over user privilege elevation for running privileged commands.

rules.title: The latest version of pam is installed
rules.explanation: The pam package implements Pluggable Authentication Modules.
rules.impact: An outdated version of pam may contain known vulnerabilities in the authentication mechanism.

rules.title: The latest version of authselect is installed
rules.explanation: The authselect utility manages PAM profiles and their consistency.
rules.impact: An outdated version of authselect may contain defects that lead to an incorrect PAM configuration.

rules.title: The latest version of libpwquality is installed
rules.explanation: The libpwquality library implements password quality checking.
rules.impact: An outdated version of libpwquality may fail to enforce the required password complexity limits.

rules.title: PAM is managed by an active authselect profile
rules.explanation: authselect generates the system-auth and password-auth files that PAM uses at runtime.
rules.impact: Manually editing PAM files while bypassing authselect makes the configuration inconsistent and can disable required checks.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock.so module keeps a per-user list of failed authentication attempts over a defined interval and locks the account when the configured number of consecutive failed authentications is exceeded.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed login attempts reduces the effectiveness of password-guessing attacks on your systems.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module performs a password quality check.
rules.impact: Using unique, complex passwords helps increase the time and resources required to crack a password.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_history.so module stores each user's recent passwords in order to enforce password history and stop the user from alternating the same password too often.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_unix.so module is the standard Unix authentication module.
rules.impact: Requiring users to authenticate reduces the likelihood that an attacker can gain access to the system.

rules.title: The password failed attempts lockout is configured
rules.explanation: The deny=n option denies access if the number of consecutive failed authentications for that user during the most recent interval exceeds n.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed login attempts reduces the effectiveness of password-guessing attacks on your systems.

rules.title: The password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: Access is restored n seconds after the account is locked.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed login attempts reduces the effectiveness of password-guessing attacks on your systems.

rules.title: The password failed attempts lockout includes root account
rules.explanation: Even_deny_root allows the root account to be locked in the same way as ordinary accounts, and root_unlock_time=n implies Even_deny_root and allows access to the root account n seconds after the lockout. If the option is not specified, the value is the same as unlock_time.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n consecutive failed login attempts reduces the risk of password-guessing attacks on your systems.

rules.title: The password number of changed characters is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality difok parameter sets the number of characters in a password that must not be present in the old password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password increases the time and resources required to compromise it. Password complexity, or strength, measures resistance to guessing and brute-force attacks: the more complex the password, the more combinations must be tried before it is compromised.

rules.title: The password length is configured
rules.explanation: minlen is the minimum acceptable size for a new password.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from being cracked by brute-force methods.

rules.title: The password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity can be set with the minclass, dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit parameters.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from being cracked by brute-force methods.

rules.title: The password same consecutive characters is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxrepeat parameter sets the maximum number of identical consecutive characters allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password increases the time and resources required to compromise it. Password complexity, or strength, measures resistance to guessing and brute-force attacks: the more complex the password, the more combinations must be tried before it is compromised.

rules.title: The password maximum sequential characters is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxsequence option sets the maximum length of monotonic character sequences in a new password, such as 12345 or Fedcb; the check is disabled when the value is 0. Most such passwords will not pass the simplicity check unless the sequence is only a minor part of the password.
rules.impact: Using a complex password increases the time and resources required to compromise it. Password complexity, or strength, measures resistance to guessing and brute-force attacks: the more complex the password, the more combinations must be tried before it is compromised.

rules.title: The password dictionary check is enabled
rules.explanation: The dictcheck parameter sets whether words from the cracklib dictionary should be checked.
rules.impact: If the operating system allows a user to choose passwords based on dictionary words, this increases the chance of the password being cracked by creating more opportunities for successful guessing and brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The password quality is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: If the enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module returns an error on a failed check even if the user changing the password is root.
rules.impact: Using a complex password helps increase the time and resources required to crack the password.

rules.title: The password history remember is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be checked to ensure that users do not reuse recent passwords. The number of remembered passwords is set with the remember argument.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: The password history is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: If the pwhistory enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module enforces password history for the root user.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse their passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password or use a compromised password.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok, when changing a password, forces the module to set the new password supplied by a previously stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows several PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: The pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the pam_unix.so default, which prevents a user from accessing a service if their official password is empty.
rules.impact: A strong password is necessary to protect personal and confidential information from unauthorized access.

rules.title: The pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember=n argument stores the last n passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd in order to enforce password history and stop the user from alternating the same password too often.
rules.impact: The remember=n argument should be removed so that a strong password hashing algorithm is used.

rules.title: The pam_unix includes a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: A cryptographic hash function converts input of arbitrary length into output of fixed length. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of the password, turning it into another string called the hashed password.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 and Yescrypt algorithms provide a stronger hash than other algorithms Linux uses to generate password hashes, increasing the effort an attacker needs to determine local users' passwords. These changes apply only to the local system.

rules.title: The pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok, when changing a password, forces the module to set the new password supplied by a previously stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows several PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: The password expiration is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to force passwords to expire once they reach a defined age.
rules.impact: The window of opportunity for an attacker to use compromised credentials, or to successfully compromise credentials with a brute-force attack, is limited by the password lifetime.

rules.title: The minimum password days is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MIN_DAYS <N> is the minimum number of days allowed between password changes.
rules.impact: By limiting how often passwords can be changed, an administrator can prevent users from changing a password repeatedly in an attempt to bypass password reuse controls.

rules.title: The password expiration warning days is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a specified number of days.
rules.impact: Advance warning that a password will expire gives users time to think of a strong password.

rules.title: The strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD (string) defines the default encryption algorithm for encrypting passwords.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 and yescrypt algorithms provide stronger hashing than other algorithms Linux uses to generate password hashes.

rules.title: The inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE defines the number of days after a password exceeds its maximum age during which the user is expected to change that password.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security because users do not log in to notice failed login attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: All users last password change date is in the past
rules.explanation: All users must have a last password change date in the past.
rules.impact: If a user's recorded last password change date is in the future, the user may have bypassed any configured password expiration.

rules.title: The root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
rules.impact: This access must be limited to the default root account only, and only from the system console.

rules.title: The root is the only GID 0 account
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify the group to which the root account belongs.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent unprivileged users from accidentally accessing files owned by root.

rules.title: The group root is the only GID 0 group
rules.explanation: The groupmod command can be used to specify the group to which the root group belongs.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root group helps prevent unprivileged users from accidentally accessing files owned by the root group.

rules.title: The root account access is controlled
rules.explanation: There are several methods of accessing the root account directly. Without a password set, any user can gain access and therefore control of the entire system.
rules.impact: Access to root must be protected at all times.
rules.scope: root password status from passwd -S root

rules.title: The root path integrity
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command on the system and can be tricked into running programs unintentionally if PATH is not set correctly.
rules.impact: Including the current working directory (.) or another writable directory in root's execution path makes it likely that an attacker can gain superuser access by inducing an administrator running as root to execute a trojan program.

rules.title: The root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the permissions of newly created directories and files.
rules.impact: Setting a secure umask value ensures that users make a deliberate choice about their file permissions.

rules.title: The system accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: Most distributions provide a number of accounts that are used to manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that accounts which are not used by ordinary users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell.

rules.title: The accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Most distributions provide a number of accounts that are used to manage applications. In addition, an administrator may add special accounts that are not intended for interactive use.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that accounts not intended for interactive use cannot be used interactively.
rules.scope: Lock status of accounts without a valid shell

rules.title: The nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file containing the full paths of valid login shells.
rules.impact: A user can use chsh to change their configured shell. Placing nologin in /etc/shells causes any user whose shell is nologin to be treated as a full, unrestricted user.

rules.title: The default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: TMOUT is an environment parameter that defines the shell timeout in seconds.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for a user to gain unauthorized access to another user's shell session that was left unattended. It also ends the idle session and releases the resources associated with that session.

rules.title: The default user umask is configured in /etc/login.defs
rules.explanation: The UMASK parameter in /etc/login.defs sets the default permission mask for new user files.
rules.impact: An overly broad permission mask makes new files readable or modifiable by other users.

rules.title: The default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the permissions of newly created directories and files.
rules.impact: Setting a secure umask value ensures that users make a deliberate choice about their file permissions.

rules.title: The journald service is active
rules.explanation: Ensure that the systemd-journald service is enabled to capture logging events.
rules.impact: If the systemd-journald service is not enabled to start at boot, the system will not capture logging events.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote is not in use
rules.explanation: The systemd-journal-remote package allows journal records to be received from remote hosts over the network.
rules.impact: Receiving journals turns a client system into a logging server and takes it outside its operational role.

rules.title: The journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: Data from systemd-journald can be stored in volatile memory or persistently on the local server.
rules.impact: If rsyslog is the preferred method for capturing logs, all system logs must be sent to it for further processing.

rules.title: The journald log file rotation is configured
rules.explanation: Journald includes the ability to rotate log files regularly so that logs do not fill the system or become unmanageably large.
rules.impact: Keeping log files smaller and more manageable lets a system administrator easily archive those files to another system and spend less time reviewing excessively large log files.

rules.title: The journald log file access is configured
rules.explanation: Journald creates log files that do not yet exist on the system. This setting determines which permissions are applied to those newly created files.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions so that confidential data is archived and protected.

rules.title: The rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog software is recommended in environments where journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: The security improvements in rsyslog justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: After the rsyslog package is installed, ensure that the service is enabled.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not enabled to start at boot, the system will not capture logging events.

rules.title: The rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: rsyslog creates log files that do not yet exist on the system. The $FileCreateMode parameter specifies the creation mode with which rsyslog creates new files.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions so that confidential data is archived and protected.

rules.title: The access to rsyslog configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: rsyslog configuration files define how logs are routed and stored.
rules.impact: Weak permissions allow logging rules to be changed and security events to be hidden.

rules.title: The access to the /etc/rsyslog.d directory is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/rsyslog.d/ directory contains additional rsyslog configuration files.
rules.impact: Write access to the rsyslog.d directory allows the logging rules to be replaced.

rules.title: The access to the rsyslog work directory is configured
rules.explanation: The rsyslog working directory (by default /var/lib/rsyslog) is used for the service queues and temporary files.
rules.impact: Weak permissions on the working directory allow interference with log processing or reading of log contents.

rules.title: The rsyslog is not configured as a log server
rules.explanation: rsyslog can accept messages from remote hosts when the imtcp, imudp, imptcp, or imrelp modules are loaded.
rules.impact: Accepting remote messages opens a network service and expands the attack surface of a host that is not intended to collect logs.

rules.title: The rsyslog logging rules are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/rsyslog.conf file and drop-in files in /etc/rsyslog.d/ define which message classes are written to which files.
rules.impact: Without correct logging rules, authentication events, privilege elevation, and root actions are not recorded.

rules.title: The rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: rsyslog can send the log events it collects to a remote log host, or receive messages from remote hosts, which provides centralized log management.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker gains root access on the local system, log data stored on the local system can be forged or deleted.

rules.title: A rsyslog TLS network stream driver is installed
rules.explanation: Forwarding logs over TLS requires the rsyslog-gnutls or rsyslog-openssl stream driver.
rules.impact: Without a TLS driver, logs are sent across the network in the clear or are not sent at all.

rules.title: The rsyslog network forwarding uses TLS
rules.explanation: When forwarding logs to a remote server, rsyslog must use TLS with host authentication.
rules.impact: Forwarding logs without encryption allows audit data to be intercepted and substituted.

rules.title: The rsyslog TLS CA certificate is configured
rules.explanation: To authenticate the remote server, rsyslog must use a trusted CA certificate.
rules.impact: Without CA verification, the connection is vulnerable to impersonation of the log collection server.

rules.title: The rsyslog TLS client certificate is configured
rules.explanation: For mutual authentication when forwarding logs over TLS, rsyslog must present a client certificate and key.
rules.impact: Without a client certificate, the log collection server cannot confirm the authenticity of the sender.

rules.title: The logrotate is configured
rules.explanation: logrotate manages rotation, compression, and deletion of log files so that they cannot grow without limit.
rules.impact: Without rotation, logs occupy all available space and disrupt logging and other services.

rules.title: The access to all logfiles has been configured
rules.explanation: Log files contain information from many services on the local system or, in the case of a centralized log server, logs from other systems.
rules.impact: It is important that log files have the correct permissions to protect confidential data, and that only the appropriate users and groups have access to them.

rules.title: The auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the user-space component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Recording system events gives system administrators information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: The auditing for processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: Configure grub2 so that processes which can be audited can still be audited even if they start before auditd starts.
rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before auditing, so that potential malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit is configured
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit parameter defines how many auditd records can be held in the auditd queue.
rules.impact: During boot, if audit=1, the queue holds 64 records. If more than 64 records are created during boot, auditd records are lost and potential malicious activity can go unnoticed.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: Enable the auditd daemon to record system events.
rules.impact: Recording system events gives system administrators information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the maximum size of the audit log file.
rules.impact: It is important to set an appropriate size for the log files so that they do not affect the system and audit data is not lost.

rules.title: The audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter defines how to handle an audit log file that reaches its maximum size.
rules.impact: In scenarios with high security requirements, the benefits of keeping a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing it.

rules.title: The system is disabled when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon can be configured to halt the system or switch to single-user mode if there is no free space or an error is detected in the partition that contains the audit log files.
rules.impact: In scenarios with high security requirements, the risk of undetected unauthorized access or repudiation outweighs the benefit of system availability.

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs are low on space
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon can be configured to halt the system, switch to single-user mode, or send a warning message if the partition that contains the audit log files is running out of space.
rules.impact: In scenarios with high security requirements, the risk of undetected unauthorized access or repudiation outweighs the benefit of system availability.

rules.title: The modification of the /etc/sudoers file is collected
rules.explanation: Monitor changes to the scope of activity for system administrators.
rules.impact: Changes to the /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d files may indicate that unauthorized changes were made to a system administrator's scope of activity.

rules.title: The actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: sudo gives users temporary elevated privileges to perform operations either as the superuser or as another user.
rules.impact: Creating an audit log of users with temporary elevated privileges and of the operations they perform is necessary for reporting.
rules.scope: Audit rules for the execve system call

rules.title: The events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: Monitor the sudo log file.
rules.impact: Changes to /var/log/sudo.log indicate that an administrator executed a command or that the log file itself has been tampered with.
rules.scope: Audit rules for the sudo log file

rules.title: The events that modify date and time information are collected
rules.explanation: Capture events in which the system date and/or time was changed. The settings cover adjtimex (kernel clock adjustment), settimeofday (set the time using timeval and timezone structures), stime (seconds since 01.01.1970), and clock_settime (set several internal clocks and timers when system calls run); on exit, write an audit record to the configured audit log and tag the records with a unique identifier such as time-change.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time can be a sign of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: The events that modify sethostname and setdomainname are collected
rules.explanation: A change to the hostname or domain name may indicate an attempt to disguise the system.
rules.impact: Without auditing of hostname and domain changes, an attacker's actions remain unnoticed.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net files contain login banners and must not be changed without oversight.
rules.impact: An unauthorized change to the banners can be used for social engineering.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname files define local name resolution and the system name.
rules.impact: Changing these files allows traffic to be redirected to a controlled host.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/sysconfig/network and /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/ are collected
rules.explanation: The network configuration files /etc/sysconfig/network and /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/ define network parameters.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to network settings can redirect traffic or disable protections.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/NetworkManager directory are collected
rules.explanation: Record changes to network environment files or related system calls.
rules.impact: Monitoring the /etc/NetworkManager/ directory detects potential unauthorized changes to network configuration files.

rules.title: The use of privileged commands are collected
rules.explanation: Track privileged programs that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set, to determine whether unprivileged users run those commands.
rules.impact: Execution of privileged commands by unprivileged users may indicate an attempt to gain unauthorized access to the system.
rules.scope: Audit rules for setuid and setgid files

rules.title: The unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Track failed attempts to access files.
rules.impact: Failed attempts to open, create, or truncate files may indicate that a person or process is trying to gain unauthorized access to the system.
rules.scope: Audit rules for open, creat, and similar calls that return EACCES or EPERM

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/group information are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file defines group membership and the privileges associated with it.
rules.impact: Changing groups can grant a user access to resources they are not entitled to.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/passwd information are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file defines user accounts and their parameters.
rules.impact: Changing /etc/passwd can result in the creation of unauthorized accounts.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow are collected
rules.explanation: Record events that change user or group information.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to these files may indicate that the system has been compromised and that an unauthorized user is trying to hide their activity or compromise additional accounts.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/security/opasswd are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file contains user password history.
rules.impact: Substituting password history allows old passwords to be reused.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/nsswitch.conf file are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/nsswitch.conf file defines the resolution order for users, groups, and names.
rules.impact: Changing nsswitch.conf allows authentication sources to be substituted.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/pam.conf and /etc/pam.d/ information are collected
rules.explanation: The files /etc/pam.conf and /etc/pam.d/ define the system's authentication policy.
rules.impact: An unauthorized change to the PAM configuration weakens authentication and can go unnoticed.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events chmod,fchmod,fchmodat are collected
rules.explanation: Changing file permissions through chmod, fchmod, or fchmodat may indicate an attempt to escalate privileges.
rules.impact: Without auditing permission changes, preparation for privilege escalation cannot be detected.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events chown,fchown,lchown,fchownat are collected
rules.explanation: Changing file ownership through chown, fchown, lchown, or fchownat may indicate an attempt to escalate privileges.
rules.impact: Without auditing ownership changes, preparation for privilege escalation cannot be detected.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events setxattr,lsetxattr,fsetxattr,removexattr,lremovexattr,fremovexattr collected
rules.explanation: Changing extended file attributes (setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr, removexattr, lremovexattr, fremovexattr) can be used to bypass access restrictions.
rules.impact: Without auditing extended-attribute changes, a bypass of mandatory and discretionary access control cannot be detected.

rules.title: The successful file system mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Track use of the mount system call.
rules.impact: It is highly unusual for an unprivileged user to mount filesystems on the system.
rules.scope: Audit rules for the mount system call

rules.title: The session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Track session initiation events.
rules.impact: Monitoring these files for changes can alert a system administrator to logins at unusual times, which may indicate attacker activity.

rules.title: The login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Track login and logout events.
rules.impact: Monitoring login and logout events can give a system administrator information related to brute-force attacks against user logins.

rules.title: The unlink file deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Track use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes.
rules.impact: Monitoring these calls from unprivileged users can give a system administrator evidence that files and file attributes associated with protected files are being deleted improperly.
rules.scope: Audit rules for unlink and unlinkat

rules.title: The rename file deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Track system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes. This configuration monitors rename (rename a file), renameat (rename a file attribute), and renameat2 (rename a file relative to directory file-descriptor system calls), and tags them with the identifier delete.
rules.impact: Monitoring these calls from unprivileged users can give a system administrator evidence that files and file attributes associated with protected files are being deleted improperly. This audit option records all such events, so administrators must look for the specific privileged files that are deleted or changed.

rules.title: The events that modify the system's Mandatory Access Controls are collected
rules.explanation: SELinux is a mandatory access control implementation. The parameters below track any write access (possible addition, deletion, or modification of files in a directory) or attribute changes in /etc/selinux/ and /usr/share/selinux/; if another mandatory access control method is used, changes in the corresponding directories must be checked.
rules.impact: Changes to files in /etc/selinux/ and /usr/share/selinux/ may indicate that an unauthorized user is trying to alter access controls and security contexts, which can compromise the system.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful use of the chcon command.
rules.impact: The chcon command is used to change a file's security context. Without audit records specific to security and the organization's needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or identify who is responsible; audit records can be produced by various information-system components, such as a policy module or filter.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful use of the setfacl command.
rules.impact: This utility sets access control lists (ACLs) on files and directories. Without audit records that match the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or identify who is responsible; audit records can be produced by various information-system components, such as a policy module or filter.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful use of the chacl command. chacl is an IRIX compatibility command, retained for users who are familiar with it from XFS or IRIX.
rules.impact: chacl changes the ACL of a file or directory. Without audit records that match the organization's security and mission needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or identify who is responsible; audit records can be produced by various information-system components, such as a policy module or filter.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are collected
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful use of the usermod command.
rules.impact: The usermod command modifies system account files to reflect the changes specified on the command line. Without audit records specific to security and the organization's needs, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or identify who is responsible; audit records can be produced by various information-system components, such as a policy module or filter.

rules.title: The kernel module loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: Track loading and unloading of kernel modules.
rules.impact: Monitoring the use of every method of manipulating kernel modules can give system administrators evidence that an unauthorized change was made to a kernel module and may have put system security at risk.

rules.title: The kernel "init_module" and "finit_module" loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: The following system calls control module loading and unloading: init_module loads a module, and finit_module loads a module when the overhead of using cryptographically signed modules to determine module authenticity can be avoided. Any execution of module load and unload programs and these system calls writes an audit record with the modules identifier.
rules.impact: Monitoring the use of every method of manipulating kernel modules can give system administrators evidence that an unauthorized change was made to a kernel module and may put system security at risk.

rules.title: The kernel "delete_module" loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: Control loading and unloading of kernel modules. All module loading, listing, and dependency checks are performed by kmod through symbolic links; delete_module removes a module, and any execution of module load and unload programs or these system calls writes an audit record with the modules identifier.
rules.impact: Monitoring the use of every method of manipulating kernel modules can give system administrators evidence that an unauthorized change was made to a kernel module and may put system security at risk.

rules.title: The audit configuration is loaded regardless of errors
rules.explanation: Set the -c flag so auditctl continues loading rules despite an error. The exit code will not be successful if any rule fails to load.
rules.impact: By default, auditctl stops loading any further rules if it detects an error in the rules, for example when a file watch refers to a file that does not exist. That can cause auditd to start without valid rules, so it is better to load and activate every valid rule rather than a subset of them.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: Configure system auditing so that audit rules cannot be changed with auditctl.
rules.impact: In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot change the audit system to potentially hide malicious activity and then restore the audit rules.

rules.title: The running and on disk configuration is the same
rules.explanation: The audit system has both an on-disk configuration and a running configuration.
rules.impact: Differences between the current running configuration and the configuration on disk can cause unexpected problems or create a false impression that requirements are met.

rules.title: The audit log file directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: The audit log directory contains the audit log files.
rules.impact: Audit information includes all information, including audit records, audit settings, and audit reports. This information is required for a successful audit of system activity.
rules.scope: Permissions on the audit log directory from auditd.conf

rules.title: The audit log files mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.
rules.scope: Permissions on audit log files in the directory from auditd.conf

rules.title: The audit log files owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.

rules.title: The audit log files group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.
rules.impact: Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.
rules.scope: Group owner of audit log files

rules.title: The audit configuration files mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd and which events are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files can allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events.

rules.title: The audit configuration files owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd and which events are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files can allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events.

rules.title: The audit configuration files group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd and which events are audited.
rules.impact: Access to audit configuration files can allow unauthorized personnel to prevent auditing of critical events.

rules.title: The audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, among others, vendor-supplied and open-source audit tools required to view and manage system activity and audit information records successfully.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manage log data.
rules.scope: Permissions on auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, and augenrules

rules.title: The audit tools owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, among others, vendor-supplied and open-source audit tools required to view and manage system activity and audit information records successfully.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manage log data.
rules.scope: Owner of audit utilities (auditctl and related tools)

rules.title: The audit tools group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, among others, vendor-supplied and open-source audit tools required to view and manage system activity and audit information records successfully.
rules.impact: Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manage log data.
rules.scope: Group owner of audit utilities (auditctl and related tools)

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE takes a snapshot of files and directories, including modification times, permissions, and file hashes, which can then be compared with the current filesystem state to detect changes on the system.
rules.impact: Monitoring filesystem state detects compromised files so that the impact of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or altered binaries can be prevented or limited.

rules.title: The filesystem integrity is regularly checked
rules.explanation: Periodic filesystem integrity checking is required to detect changes to the filesystem.
rules.impact: Periodic checking of files lets a system administrator determine, on a regular basis, whether critical files have been modified in an unauthorized way.
rules.scope: Settings in crontab or the systemd timer aidecheck.timer

rules.title: The cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools
rules.explanation: Audit tools include, among others, vendor-supplied open-source audit tools required to view and manage audit information system activity and records successfully. Audit tools include customizable queries and report generators.
rules.impact: Protecting the integrity of tools used for auditing is an important step toward ensuring the integrity of audit information, which includes everything needed to audit information-system activity, such as audit records, audit settings, and audit reports. Attackers may replace audit tools or inject code into existing tools in order to hide or delete system activity from audit logs, so the tools must be cryptographically signed, for example with a checksum hash of the file or files, so that modification, tampering, or replacement can be detected.

rules.title: The report_url is configured
rules.explanation: The report_url directive in the AIDE configuration defines where the integrity-check report is sent.
rules.impact: Without sending the report to the system log, integrity-check results can be lost or go unnoticed.

rules.title: The access to /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user account information used by many system utilities, so it must be readable for those utilities to work.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect /etc/passwd from unauthorized write access.

rules.title: The access to /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user account information used by many system utilities, so it must be readable for those utilities to work.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect /etc/passwd from unauthorized write access.

rules.title: The access to /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains a list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file must be protected from unauthorized changes by unprivileged users, but it must remain readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: The access to /etc/group- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains a list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file must be protected from unauthorized changes by unprivileged users, but it must remain readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: The access to /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: The access to /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file containing the full paths of valid login shells.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect /etc/shells from unauthorized access.

rules.title: The access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/security/opasswd and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old store users' previous passwords if the system uses pam_unix or pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: It is essential to protect /etc/security/opasswd from unauthorized access.

rules.title: The world writable files and directories are secured
rules.explanation: World-writable files are the least secure.
rules.impact: Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World-writable files may also indicate an incorrectly written script or program that could cause a more serious compromise of system integrity.

rules.title: No files or directories without an owner and a group exist
rules.explanation: Administrators may remove users or groups from the system and fail to delete all files and directories owned by those users or groups.
rules.impact: A new user or group that is assigned the user ID or group ID of a removed user can end up as the owner of the removed user's or group's files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are reviewed
rules.explanation: A file owner can set the file to execute with the owner's or the group's privileges even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group.
rules.impact: There are valid reasons for SUID and SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate.
rules.scope: SUID and SGID files on the system

rules.title: The accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts can use shadowed passwords.
rules.impact: The /etc/passwd file also contains information such as user and group identifiers, which is used by many system programs. Therefore /etc/passwd must remain readable by all users.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field means that anyone can log in as that user without entering a password.
rules.impact: All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent an unauthorized user from using the account.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group permissions are not managed properly.
rules.impact: Groups defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group pose a threat to system security because group permissions are not managed properly.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: User groups must be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: Users must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Groups must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.
rules.impact: Groups must be assigned unique names to ensure accountability and appropriate access protections.

rules.title: The local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: A user's home directory is space defined for that user to set local environment variables and store personal files. An administrator can set secure permissions on users' home directories, but users can easily override them, and users may be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory or with a home directory that does not actually exist.
rules.impact: Because the user is responsible for files stored in the home directory, the user must own the directory. Group or publicly accessible home directories can let attackers steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges, and if the home directory does not exist or is not assigned, the user is placed in / and cannot write any files or set local environment variables.

rules.title: The local interactive user dot files access is configured
rules.explanation: User configuration files with excessive or incorrect permissions can let attackers steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.
rules.impact: User configuration files with excessive or incorrect permissions can let attackers steal or modify other users' data or obtain another user's system privileges.
rules.scope: Permissions on user dot files (.bashrc, .profile, and similar) in home directories
